736.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
736.hook: a shepherd boy with a sling and no armor faces a giant
736.howItsDone: Jews read David and Goliath as part of the Former Prophets, and many readers take it as a story of courage and of trust in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's harp, and a king whose dark lifted. Your line was music lifts. Today, the same shepherd, with a very different tool in his hand.

Two armies on two mountains, a valley between them. Morning and evening, a Philistine champion named Goliath walks out into that valley in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam, and shouts: choose a man, and let him come down to me. Saul and all Israel are dismayed and greatly afraid. Into this walks the youngest son of Jesse, sent by his father to bring bread to his older brothers at the front. He hears the challenge, and asks: who is this, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `CHOOSE A MAN, AND LET HIM COME.` → `A BOY BRINGING BREAD.`

segments.voice: His oldest brother, Eliab, is furious: why did you come down here? I know your pride. But word reaches Saul, and David says: your servant will go and fight him. You're a boy, says Saul, and he's been a man of war since his youth. David answers from experience. When a lion or a bear took a lamb from the flock, I went after it and took the lamb from its mouth. The LORD who saved me from the lion and the bear will save me from this Philistine. So Saul dresses David in his own armor: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, a sword. David tries to walk, and can't. I haven't tried these, he says, and takes them off. This is the heart of the story. He doesn't go out in the king's equipment, pretending to be a soldier. He goes out as what he is. He takes his staff, and "chose him five smooth stones out of the brook," puts them in his shepherd's bag, sling in hand. Goliath mocks him. David answers: you come to me with a sword and a spear, "but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts," for the battle is the LORD's. He runs toward the Philistine, takes one stone, slings it, and it sinks into Goliath's forehead, and he falls on his face. The text even notes there was no sword in David's hand. He picked five, and needed one.

segments.voice: Name one giant in your valley right now, a debt, a hard conversation, a project you can't start, and notice whether you've been fighting it in someone else's armor. Then ask what your smooth stones are, the small things you already know how to do, and choose one. If you pray, bring the giant to God as David did.

737.title: As his own soul (1 Samuel 18:1–4)
737.hook: Jonathan loves David as his own soul and gives him his robe
737.howItsDone: Jews read the friendship of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot about love that depends on nothing is studied with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday a shepherd with a sling and no armor walked out to meet a giant. Your line was one was enough. Today, someone standing near the king is watching him.

The fight is over. David stands before King Saul, who asks a plain question: whose son are you? The son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem. That's all David says, as far as the text tells us. But someone else is in the room: Jonathan, the king's son. A fighter himself, who once climbed a rocky pass with only his armor-bearer to face a Philistine camp. Later, Saul will tell him outright that as long as David lives, Jonathan's own kingdom won't be secure. Jonathan has every reason to see a rival. And when David has finished speaking, the text turns from the king and looks at his son.
screen: `WHOSE SON ARE YOU?` → `JONATHAN IS LISTENING.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND A RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Chapter eighteen opens: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, "and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." The Hebrew word under soul is nefesh, and it's wider than the English: life, breath, the self that's alive in you. Jonathan loves David the way a person holds on to their own life. And the phrase comes twice. Two verses later Jonathan makes a covenant with David, a binding promise, and the reason given is the same: he loved him as his own soul. Then he strips off his robe and gives it to David. Then his garments, his sword, his bow, his belt. Everything a prince and a soldier would wear, handed to a shepherd. The text doesn't explain the gesture. Some readers hear the heir quietly handing over what marks him as heir. Others hear a friend dressing his friend in the best he has. Either way, nothing comes back: David gives nothing in these verses. The rabbis noticed this friendship. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, teaches that love which depends on some thing ends when the thing is gone, and love which depends on nothing never ends. Its example of the second kind is the love of David and Jonathan: a friendship that isn't about what the other person can do for you.

segments.voice: Let one friend come to mind, someone whose life you'd hold close. Look around your own life for something to hand them, not something you were throwing out, but a book you love, an hour, a thing you made, and picture putting it in their hands. If part of you wants to hold it back, let that be there too; if you pray, you can hold the verse, he loved him as his own soul.

738.title: Through the window (1 Samuel 19:11–17)
738.hook: Michal lets David down through a window to escape her father
738.howItsDone: Jews read Michal's rescue of David in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; Psalm 59, whose heading ties it to this night, is read in the book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday the king's son gave a shepherd his robe, his sword and his bow. Your line was love that doesn't end. Today, the king's daughter saves the same man's life.

Night, and there are men outside the house. King Saul has sent them to watch David's door and kill him in the morning. Inside are David and his wife, Michal, Saul's own daughter. A chapter earlier the text said plainly that Michal loved David. Now she tells him: if you don't save your life tonight, tomorrow you'll be killed. The front door is watched. She has a house, a husband, a father who is the king, and maybe a few hours. What she does next happens at a window.
screen: `MEN WATCH THE DOOR.` → `SAUL'S DAUGHTER, DAVID'S WIFE.` → `TONIGHT, OR NOT AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The verse is short and fast: "So Michal let David down through the window; and he went, and fled, and escaped." Three verbs for David, like footsteps. Then Michal turns back into the room and buys him time. She lays the household image the text calls teraphim in the bed, puts a pillow of goats' hair where his head would be, and covers it with a cloth. When Saul's messengers come, she says David is sick. Saul sends them back: bring him to me in the bed, so I can kill him. They pull back the cover and find the image and the goats' hair. Now Michal is the one facing her father. Why did you deceive me and let my enemy escape? She answers with a story: David said to her, let me go, why should I kill you? It may not be true; the text doesn't say. It reads like a daughter shielding herself from a father who has already thrown a spear at David. So the window works two ways. It's how David gets out, and it's where Michal stays behind. Her rescue costs her something, and the story lets her pay it alone. One small echo: the heading of Psalm fifty-nine ties that psalm to this very night, when Saul sent men to watch the house. A prayer, by tradition, from inside the danger she helped him out of.

segments.voice: Danger doesn't always look like men at the door: a friend in a bad stretch, a coworker getting blamed, a kid being picked on. Let one person come to mind, and look for the window, the one small opening you could give them: a call, a word to the right person, a ride. If you pray, you can hold that person by name.

739.title: The arrows (1 Samuel 20)
739.hook: Jonathan signals with arrows, and the friends part in tears
739.howItsDone: Jews read the parting of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the chapter's feast of the new moon, Rosh Chodesh, is still marked in the Jewish calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday Michal lowered David through the window and stayed behind. Your line was she stayed behind. Today, a signal in a field.

A code, worked out in advance between two friends who can't risk being seen talking. David will hide in a field, beside a stone. Jonathan will come out as if for target practice, with a boy to fetch his arrows, and shoot three arrows to the side. If he shouts that the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe: come home. If he shouts that they're beyond you, the king means to kill him: go. Jonathan has to find out which at his father's table, at the feast of the new moon. Then he must say it aloud, in front of a boy who has no idea what it means.
screen: `DAVID HIDES BY THE STONE.` → `THREE ARROWS AND A BOY.` → `THIS SIDE, OR BEYOND?`

segments.voice: At the feast, David's seat is empty. On the second day Saul asks, and Jonathan covers for his friend. Saul explodes. He shames his own son, tells him that as long as David lives, Jonathan's kingdom won't stand, and throws a spear at him. Now Jonathan knows. In the morning he goes out to the field. The boy runs, Jonathan shoots past him, and calls the line they agreed on: "Behold, the arrows are beyond thee." The answer is go. Then he adds, as if to a slow servant: make speed, hurry, don't stay. The words are for the boy, and for the man behind the stone. And here the plan breaks down, in the best way. The code was built so they wouldn't have to meet. Jonathan sends the boy back to town with his weapons. David comes out and bows to the ground. They kiss and weep together, and the text says David wept the more. Jonathan's last words are a blessing and a promise: go in peace. We have sworn in the name of the Lord that the Lord will be between me and you, and between my children and your children, for ever. He doesn't say goodbye by signal, or by pretending it's fine. He sends the witness away and says it face to face. The arrows told David everything he needed to know. The goodbye told him something the arrows couldn't.

740.title: Sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24)
740.hook: David cuts Saul's robe in the cave but will not harm him
740.carry: I will not put forth my hand
740.howItsDone: Jews read David sparing Saul in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and some teachers read it alongside the Torah's warnings against taking revenge or bearing a grudge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arrows past a boy in a field, and two friends weeping goodbye. Your line was the arrows are beyond thee. Today, David is on the run, and the king walks into his hiding place.

A cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, wild-goat country. Deep inside, in the dark, David and his men are hiding from the king who wants him dead. Then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself, with no idea who's at the back of the cave. David's men lean in and whisper: this is the day God promised. Your enemy, delivered into your hand. Do to him whatever seems good to you. David gets up, and creeps forward in the dark.
screen: `A CAVE AT EN-GEDI.` → `THE KING WALKS IN ALONE.` → `THIS IS THE DAY, THEY SAY.`

segments.voice: He reaches Saul and quietly cuts off the corner of his robe. That's all. And then, the text says, David's heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt. Robes matter in this book. Earlier, when Saul grabbed the prophet Samuel's robe and it tore, Samuel told him the kingdom had been torn from him the same way. So a torn corner of the king's robe is no small thing. David turns to his men: God forbid. I will not put forth my hand against my lord, because he is the Lord's anointed. He holds them back, and Saul walks out unharmed. Then David takes a risk. He follows, calls after Saul, bows to the ground, and holds up the corner of the robe. I was close enough to cut this, and I didn't kill you. Let the Lord judge between us, but my hand won't be on you. And Saul, the hunter, weeps aloud. Is this your voice, my son David? He says David is more righteous than he is, because David repaid him good for evil. Here's what makes this hard. David's men use religious language: this is the day God promised. David answers with religious language too: the Lord's anointed. Same God, opposite conclusions. The text sides with the one who keeps his hand still, and it notices that even the small cut hurt his conscience.

741.title: Abigail (1 Samuel 25)
741.hook: a wise woman stops David's rage with food and words
741.howItsDone: Jews read Abigail's story in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the Talmud remembers her among the women it counts as prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cave, a king alone, and a corner of his robe. Your line was I will not put forth my hand. Today, David nearly doesn't hold back, and someone stops him.
screen: `I WILL NOT PUT FORTH MY HAND.`

segments.voice: "Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse?" That's the answer David's young men bring back. They had gone politely to a rich sheep owner named Nabal at shearing time, a time of feasting. David's band had camped near Nabal's shepherds in the wilderness and kept them safe; now they asked for whatever he could spare. Nabal sends them off with an insult. David says one thing to his men: gird on your swords, and he buckles on his own. By the time a servant runs to tell Nabal's wife, David is already on the road, and he's not coming to talk.
screen: `SHEARING TIME AT CARMEL.` → `WHO IS DAVID?` → `GIRD ON YOUR SWORDS.`

segments.voice: The servant tells Abigail everything. The text calls her a woman of good understanding, and her husband churlish. She doesn't wait, and she doesn't tell Nabal. She loads donkeys with bread and wine, meat and grain, raisins and figs, and rides out. She meets David coming down a mountain path. He has already sworn that by morning no male of Nabal's house will be left. Abigail gets off her donkey, falls at his feet, and says: upon me, my lord, let the blame be. Each step of her speech counts. She doesn't defend her husband; his name means fool, she says, and folly is with him. She takes the fault on herself. Then she looks past today. When God has made you ruler over Israel, you won't want this on your heart: blood shed for nothing, saving yourself with your own hand. She gives an angry man a picture of who he'll want to have been. And David stops. Blessed be the Lord who sent you to meet me, he says, "and blessed be thy discretion," and blessed be you, who kept me from bloodguilt. The Hebrew for discretion is ta'am, which also means taste: the sense to tell what fits the moment. Not a soldier, not one of his own men: a woman with food and the right words turned him from rage to blessing. The rabbis of the Talmud remember her among the women of Israel they count as prophets.

Abigail. The woman of good understanding who rode out with bread and wine, met David's rage on a mountain path, and turned it. Today's word.

742.title: The woman of Endor (1 Samuel 28)
742.hook: desperate Saul consults a medium, who then insists on feeding him
742.tomorrow: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1:17–27)
742.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's night at Endor in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the Torah forbids consulting mediums and the dead, and commentators have debated what happened in the woman's house.

segments.voice: Yesterday Abigail talked David down from bloodshed. Your line was blessed be thy discretion. Today, another woman, another meal, and a king at the end of his rope.

Samuel is dead and buried. The Philistine army is camped across the valley, and when Saul sees it, his heart trembles greatly. He asks God what to do, and nothing comes. No dream. No answer by the Urim, the priest's lots. No prophet. So the king does the thing he himself had outlawed. Saul had driven the mediums and ghost-raisers out of the land. Now he tells his servants: find me a woman who can call up the dead. There's one at Endor. Saul puts on other clothes, and goes by night.
screen: `SAMUEL IS DEAD.` → `NO DREAM, NO URIM, NO PROPHET.` → `BY NIGHT, TO ENDOR.`

segments.voice: The woman is wary. You know what Saul did to people like me, she says; are you setting a trap? The disguised king swears by the Lord she won't be punished, and asks for Samuel. When she sees what comes up, she screams, because now she knows who her visitor is. She describes an old man coming up, wrapped in a robe. Readers have argued over what really happened in that room, and the text doesn't settle it. What it gives is Samuel's message, and it is crushing. The kingdom has been torn from you. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Saul falls full length on the ground, no strength left; he hasn't eaten all day or all night. Here the story turns. The woman goes to him. I took my life in my hand and listened to you, she says. Now listen to me. Let me set a bit of bread before you, so you'll have strength for the road. He refuses. His servants join in, and she keeps pressing, until he gets up off the floor and sits on the bed. She moves fast. She kills the fatted calf in the house, kneads flour, bakes flat bread, and sets it before Saul and his servants. They eat, and go out into the night. The Torah forbids what she does for a living. And the text still lets her be the one who shows Saul kindness that night.
screen: `ARE YOU SETTING A TRAP?` · `AN OLD MAN IN A ROBE.` · `SAUL FALLS. NO STRENGTH LEFT.` · then, large: `SHE FED HIM.` · then: `THE CALF, THE BREAD, THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who's on the floor right now: grieving, exhausted, scared, out of options. The woman of Endor didn't argue with Saul's fear or fix his future; she put bread in front of him, so think what the bread would be for your person, a meal at the door, coffee, sitting with them while they eat. If you pray, you can hold their name.
medium. The woman at Endor the king had once outlawed, who saw Saul fall and wouldn't let him leave hungry. Today's word.
Your line: she fed him. Looking back on the week: smooth stones, nefesh, window, the arrows, sparing Saul, Abigail, and the medium of Endor. Day seven hundred forty-two.
